question: What made you want to study landscape architecture?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific story connecting personal experience to the discipline, not a vague love of nature.

bullets: Name a concrete moment or place that sparked the interest
Show you understand it as a design discipline, not just gardening or planting
Connect the interest to what you actually want to do with it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It started when my town redid the riverside park near my house, and I watched a muddy strip turn into somewhere people actually gathered. I got curious about who decides where a bench goes or why one path feels welcoming and another doesn't, and that led me to landscape architecture rather than just gardening. What hooked me was realizing it sits between ecology, engineering and design, and that combination is exactly what I want to spend years learning.

commonMistakes: Saying only that they love nature or being outdoors
Confusing the course with horticulture or garden design
Giving no specific place or project that triggered the interest
followUps: Have you visited that park again since, and what would you change about it now?

question: How would you explain the difference between landscape architecture and architecture to someone who has never heard of it?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of scope and subject matter, not just 'one is buildings and one is outside'.

bullets: State that architecture designs buildings while landscape architecture designs the outdoor and open spaces around and between them
Mention that landscape architecture works with living, changing systems like plants, water and soil, not just fixed materials
Note the overlap, since the two disciplines have to work together on most real sites
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Architecture is mostly about the building itself, its structure, its interior, how people move through it. Landscape architecture takes on everything around that building and beyond it, the paths, planting, drainage, public space, and it has to think about things that grow and change over decades, not just get built once and stay fixed. On a real project the two disciplines are constantly talking to each other, because a beautiful building surrounded by a badly designed car park still fails.

commonMistakes: Saying landscape architecture is just gardening at a bigger scale
Ignoring the ecological and time-based dimension of the work
Treating the two disciplines as unrelated rather than collaborative
followUps: Can you think of a building you know where the surrounding landscape lets it down or lifts it up?

subtopic: Landscape architecture vs gardening or horticulture
question: People often assume landscape architecture is just fancy gardening. What would you say to that?
lookingFor: Ability to defend the discipline's design and technical range without dismissing horticulture.

bullets: Respect horticulture and planting knowledge as genuinely part of the field, not beneath it
Explain the wider scope: grading, drainage, materials, masterplanning, policy, public consultation
Give an example of a project where planting is only a small piece of the design problem
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would not dismiss gardening, plant knowledge is actually a real skill landscape architects need. But a landscape architect might also be working out how water drains across a whole housing site, choosing paving that survives flooding, or running consultation with residents about a park nobody trusts yet. A project like a flood defence scheme that doubles as a public walkway shows how much engineering, ecology and community thinking sits alongside the planting.

commonMistakes: Being dismissive or snobbish about horticulture
Only listing planting-related tasks as if that is the whole job
Failing to give a concrete example of the broader scope
followUps: What technical skills do you think a landscape architect needs beyond plant knowledge?

subtopic: A landscape or public space they admire
question: Tell us about a landscape or public space you admire and why it works.
lookingFor: First-hand observation and the ability to analyse design choices, not just name a famous park.

bullets: Pick a place they have actually visited or studied closely, ideally with a specific memory
Point to a concrete design decision, materials, layout, planting, sightlines, rather than a vague feeling
Explain why that decision works for the people who use the space
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to the High Line in New York, partly because of the wider story but mostly because of one detail, how the planting is deliberately loose and grassy so it still reads as the old railway even though it is completely designed. The sunken seating pods let you sit below the sightline of the crowd, which makes a narrow strip feel much less crowded than it actually is. It taught me that a strong concept, in that case memory of the site, can guide hundreds of small decisions and keep the whole thing coherent.

commonMistakes: Naming a famous space with only surface-level praise
Never having actually visited or researched the place in depth
Describing what the space looks like without explaining why it functions well
followUps: Is there anything about that space you think does not work as well?

question: Walk us through one piece in your portfolio and the thinking behind it.
lookingFor: Evidence of a design process, not just a finished pretty image, and honest reflection on weaknesses.

bullets: Describe the brief or starting problem before the final image
Show the process, sketches, iterations, decisions that changed along the way
Reflect honestly on what they would improve if they did it again
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One piece was a redesign of a neglected pocket park near my school for an art project. I started with a site visit and just sat there for an hour noting who actually used it and how, which changed my plan completely because I had assumed families and it was mostly teenagers cutting through. My early sketches had a big central lawn, but I moved it to the edge once I saw the desire lines people had already worn into the grass. Looking back I would have tested the seating layout with actual measurements instead of guessing the scale.

commonMistakes: Presenting only the final render with no process shown
Being unable to explain why any design decision was made
Refusing to admit any weakness in the work
followUps: What would you do differently if you revisited that project today?

question: What role do you think landscape architects play in tackling problems like biodiversity loss or urban flooding?
lookingFor: Understanding that landscape architecture sits at the front line of environmental problem-solving, with a specific example.

bullets: Explain that landscape architects shape land use decisions that directly affect habitat and water flow
Give a specific technique or example, such as rain gardens, green roofs, wetland restoration
Acknowledge the tension between environmental goals and budget, maintenance or development pressure
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Landscape architects are often the ones deciding what happens to the ground itself, so choices like using permeable paving or a rain garden instead of a drain can genuinely reduce flooding on a street. I read about swales being used on a housing development to slow water down before it reaches the sewer system, which struck me as such a simple, elegant fix. What I find hardest to reconcile is that the most ecologically rich option is not always the cheapest to maintain, and part of the job seems to be arguing that case to a client.

commonMistakes: Vague claims about 'helping the planet' with no mechanism given
No awareness of any real technique like sustainable drainage or green infrastructure
Ignoring cost or maintenance trade-offs entirely
followUps: How would you convince a cost-conscious client to spend more on a sustainable drainage feature?

question: If you were given a site to design for the first time, what would you want to find out before you started drawing anything?
lookingFor: A structured, realistic approach to site analysis rather than jumping straight to a design idea.

bullets: Mention physical factors: topography, soil, drainage, sun path, existing planting
Mention human factors: who uses the site now, access, how people already move through it
Show awareness that constraints, budget, planning rules, client brief, shape the design as much as opportunities
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Before drawing anything I would want to walk the site at different times of day to see how light and use change, and check things like which way it slopes, whether it floods, and what is already growing there. I would also want to know who actually uses the space now, because desire paths and worn grass tell you more honestly than any survey what people actually want. Only after that would I start looking at the brief's constraints, budget and any planning restrictions, so the design responds to a real place rather than an assumption of one.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to describing a design idea with no analysis first
Only mentioning physical site factors and ignoring how people use the space
Forgetting that budget and planning constraints shape real projects
followUps: What would you do if the site visit revealed something the client's brief had not mentioned at all?

question: What do you understand by the idea of 'sense of place', and why does it matter in landscape design?
lookingFor: Ability to engage with a genuinely conceptual idea in the field and ground it with a real example.

bullets: Define it in their own words as the particular character and meaning a place holds for the people connected to it
Explain why ignoring it produces generic, placeless design
Give a real or hypothetical example of a design that either respects or destroys it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand sense of place as the specific character a location has, its history, materials, light, the way local people already relate to it, rather than treating it as a blank site that could be anywhere. If you ignore it you end up with the same paved plaza with the same three tree species that could be dropped into any city centre, and it never quite feels like it belongs. I think about a regeneration scheme near me that kept the old mill's brick wall as a boundary feature instead of demolishing it, which cost more but meant the new park still felt like it grew out of that specific town's history.

commonMistakes: Reciting the term without a clear definition in their own words
Giving no concrete example to ground the idea
Confusing sense of place with simply adding local plant species
followUps: Can a completely new site, with no history, ever have a sense of place?

question: How would you design a park that has to work for both toddlers and teenagers at the same time?
lookingFor: Practical design reasoning about conflicting user needs, showing empathy for both groups.

bullets: Recognise the conflicting needs, supervision and safety for one group, independence and space for the other
Suggest a concrete spatial solution, zoning, sightlines, different equipment or surfaces
Show awareness that overlap and shared space can also be valuable, not just separation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A toddler space needs to be enclosed, visible to parents on a bench, and soft underfoot, while teenagers usually want somewhere slightly out of adult sightlines where they can hang out on their own terms. I would zone the park so the toddler area sits near the entrance with clear sightlines back to parking and seating, and put something like a basketball court or informal seating steps further in, screened a bit by planting. I would still want a shared central lawn or path so the two groups are not completely cut off from each other, because a park that is only zones can feel fragmented.

commonMistakes: Designing only for one age group and ignoring the other
Suggesting a generic solution with no spatial reasoning behind it
Treating conflict between users as unsolvable rather than a design problem
followUps: What would you do if a nearby resident objected to the teenage area because of noise?

question: Landscape architects often design spaces for communities they are not part of. How would you make sure a design actually reflects what local people want?
lookingFor: Awareness that good design depends on genuine listening, not assuming you know best.

bullets: Mention concrete consultation methods, workshops, surveys, walking the site with residents
Acknowledge that different groups within a community can want conflicting things
Show humility, that the designer's job is to interpret and balance input, not just impose a personal vision
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would want to actually go and talk to people who use the space now, not just circulate a form, because a lot of what matters comes out in conversation rather than a tick box. I know different groups will want different things, so part of the job is being honest about trade-offs rather than promising everyone gets exactly what they asked for. I read about a project where the designers ran workshops with kids using models made of cardboard, and I liked that it let people who cannot read a plan still genuinely shape the outcome.

commonMistakes: Assuming a survey alone counts as meaningful consultation
Ignoring that community members can disagree with each other
Suggesting the designer's personal taste should override what people actually said
followUps: What would you do if the community consultation results contradicted the client's brief?

question: What technical or drawing skills do you think you will need to develop for this course?
lookingFor: Realistic awareness of the balance between hand skills and digital tools in the discipline.

bullets: Mention both hand-drawing or model-making and digital tools such as CAD or GIS
Show honesty about what they already know and what they expect to learn
Understand that these are means to communicate design ideas, not the end goal
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I already sketch a fair amount by hand, which I think is useful for thinking quickly on a site visit, but I know I will need to get properly comfortable with software like CAD and probably GIS for mapping and analysis at a bigger scale. I have only played with basic design software so far, so I expect that to be a steep but useful learning curve. What I care about most is that the drawing, whichever tool, actually communicates an idea clearly, rather than just looking polished.

commonMistakes: Claiming expert-level skill in every piece of software
Treating software fluency as the whole point of the course rather than a tool
Dismissing hand sketching as outdated or unnecessary
followUps: Have you used any mapping or GIS tools before, even informally?

question: What do you think a good planting design has to consider, beyond just which plants look nice together?
lookingFor: Practical understanding that planting design is functional and technical, not purely decorative.

bullets: Mention growing conditions, soil, light, moisture, and how they suit particular species
Mention how planting changes over time, seasonality, growth rate, maintenance needs
Mention function beyond appearance, screening, habitat, erosion control, shade
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A planting design has to match the actual conditions of the site, a plant that looks great in a catalogue can die within a year if the soil or drainage is wrong for it. It also has to account for time, since a newly planted scheme looks nothing like it will in five or ten years, and someone has to be able to realistically maintain it. Beyond looks, planting can do real work, screening an ugly view, holding a slope together, or supporting pollinators, so I try to think about what job each plant is doing, not just its colour.

commonMistakes: Talking only about colour, texture or aesthetic combinations
Ignoring how planting matures and changes over years
Forgetting maintenance requirements and realistic upkeep
followUps: Can you name a plant you think is overused in public planting schemes, and why?

question: Can you explain what is meant by 'hard landscape' and 'soft landscape'?
lookingFor: A basic, correct grasp of core terminology used constantly in the discipline.

bullets: Define hard landscape as built, non-living elements like paving, walls, steps, structures
Define soft landscape as living elements like planting, lawns, trees, soil
Note that the two are designed together, not separately
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Hard landscape is the built, non-living part of a scheme, things like paving, retaining walls, steps and seating. Soft landscape is the living part, planting, lawns, trees, anything that grows and changes. In practice you cannot really design one without the other, because a path's material affects how water drains into the planting bed next to it, so a good scheme treats them as one connected system rather than separate jobs.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which term refers to which element
Describing them as entirely unrelated design decisions
Giving no examples of what falls under each category
followUps: Can you give an example of a hard and soft landscape decision that had to work together?

question: What is a sustainable drainage system, and why might a landscape architect want to use one instead of a normal storm drain?
lookingFor: Basic technical knowledge of a genuinely common concept in the field, with the reasoning behind it.

bullets: Explain the basic idea: slowing, storing or filtering rainwater near where it falls instead of piping it away fast
Give an example, swales, rain gardens, permeable paving, retention ponds
Explain the benefit, reduced flood risk downstream, water quality, habitat, amenity value
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A sustainable drainage system tries to manage rainwater close to where it falls, slowing it down and letting it soak in or filter naturally, instead of just piping it straight into the sewer as fast as possible. Things like swales, rain gardens or permeable paving are common examples I have read about. I find it appealing because it does several jobs at once, it reduces flood risk further downstream, improves water quality before it reaches a river, and can double as an attractive planted feature rather than a hidden pipe.

commonMistakes: Not knowing any concrete example of a sustainable drainage feature
Describing it purely as an environmental nicety with no practical benefit explained
Confusing it with a completely different water feature like a fountain
followUps: What might a client object to about using a sustainable drainage system instead of a conventional drain?

question: Why does the slope or level of a site matter so much in landscape design?
lookingFor: Basic technical grasp of how topography drives design decisions, not just an aesthetic answer.

bullets: Explain that slope affects drainage, water always moves downhill and design has to account for that
Explain that slope affects accessibility, steep gradients can exclude wheelchair users or pushchairs
Mention that changing levels, terracing, retaining walls, ramps, is itself a design and cost decision
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Slope decides where water naturally wants to go, so if you ignore it you end up with paths that flood or planting beds that erode. It also directly affects who can use a space, a steep ramp or set of steps with no alternative shuts out wheelchair users, older people, or anyone with a pushchair. Changing the levels with terracing or retaining walls can solve that, but it is expensive, so reading the existing topography properly at the start saves a lot of cost and awkward fixes later.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning aesthetics like views, without technical reasoning
Ignoring accessibility implications of gradient
Assuming levels can always be freely changed with no cost consequence
followUps: How would you make a steep site accessible without turning it into a huge, dominant ramp?

question: How is landscape architecture different from urban planning, and where do the two overlap?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of adjacent disciplines and how they collaborate on real projects.

bullets: Describe urban planning as concerned with policy, land use and the bigger strategic picture of a city or region
Describe landscape architecture as more directly involved in the physical design of specific spaces
Note where the two meet, masterplans, public realm strategies, green infrastructure networks
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Urban planning tends to operate at the policy and land use level, deciding what kind of development goes where across a whole city, while landscape architecture gets much more into the physical design of specific spaces within that framework, how a street or a park actually looks and functions. They overlap heavily on things like masterplans or green infrastructure strategies, where a planner might set the target for green space per resident and a landscape architect works out what that space is and how it connects across the site.

commonMistakes: Treating the two disciplines as interchangeable
Describing planning as only about buildings, with no mention of land use policy
Giving no example of where the two disciplines actually meet on a project
followUps: Which of the two feels closer to what you want to do, and why?

question: Is there a landscape architect or designed landscape from history that has influenced how you think about the subject?
lookingFor: Evidence of wider reading beyond the syllabus and genuine engagement with the discipline's history.

bullets: Name a real designer or landscape with at least basic factual accuracy
Explain specifically what about their work or approach influenced their thinking
Connect it back to something they want to apply in their own future work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read about Frederick Law Olmsted's work on Central Park and what struck me was that it was never meant to look designed, he wanted it to feel like an escape from the city that just happened to exist within it. That idea, that the most successful design can hide its own hand, has stuck with me and made me pay much more attention to how 'natural' looking spaces are often the most carefully engineered ones. It has made me want to study how much intention sits behind spaces that look effortless.

commonMistakes: Naming a designer with clearly incorrect facts about their work
Giving a name with no explanation of what specifically influenced them
Reciting a textbook summary with no personal reflection
followUps: Is there anything about that designer's approach you would disagree with today?

question: How do you think climate change is changing the way landscapes need to be designed?
lookingFor: Ability to connect a big global issue to specific, practical design implications.

bullets: Mention a concrete pressure, more intense rainfall, drought, heat, rising sea level, and how it changes design
Give a specific adaptation response, drought-tolerant planting, shade strategies, flood-resilient layouts
Show awareness this is not hypothetical, but already shaping real projects
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One thing I keep noticing is that planting palettes are changing, species that used to be reliable in a region are struggling with hotter, drier summers, so designers are having to plant for the climate a place will have in thirty years, not the one it has now. Heat is another one, more cities are having to design streets and squares with real shade strategies, tree canopy, shade structures, because heatwaves are becoming genuinely dangerous in paved areas. It feels like climate change has turned what used to be a background consideration into one of the central design drivers on almost every brief.

commonMistakes: Giving only a generic statement about climate change with no design implication
Naming no specific technique or adaptation strategy
Treating the issue as a future problem rather than one already affecting current design
followUps: What would you do if a client insisted on a planting scheme you knew would not survive the changing climate?

question: What would you do if the most beautiful design option was not the most practical one?
lookingFor: Mature design judgement that weighs competing priorities rather than defaulting to either extreme.

bullets: Acknowledge that both beauty and function genuinely matter, rather than dismissing one
Describe a process for weighing them, cost, maintenance, safety, longevity against visual impact
Show willingness to compromise or find a hybrid solution rather than picking one side blindly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I do not think I would just pick one over the other automatically, I would want to understand exactly why the beautiful option was less practical, whether that is cost, maintenance, or something like safety. Sometimes a slightly less dramatic material choice can still capture most of the visual intent while actually being something the client can maintain for twenty years. I would rather find that middle option than deliver something stunning on day one that gets ripped out in five years because nobody could look after it.

commonMistakes: Claiming aesthetics should always win with no acknowledgement of practicality
Claiming practicality should always win with no value placed on design quality
Giving no real process for how they would actually resolve the tension
followUps: Can you think of a real example where you think a designer got that balance wrong?

question: What factors would you think about when choosing a paving material for a public path?
lookingFor: Practical, grounded reasoning about materials rather than a purely visual answer.

bullets: Mention durability and how the material handles weather, wear and foot traffic over time
Mention accessibility, a surface has to be even and safe underfoot, especially when wet
Mention cost, maintenance and sourcing alongside how it looks
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would want something durable enough to survive heavy footfall and weather without cracking or becoming slippery, especially somewhere that gets a lot of rain or frost. Accessibility matters a lot too, an uneven or overly textured surface can genuinely be a barrier for wheelchair users or anyone less steady on their feet. Cost and how easy it is to repair a damaged section also factor in, because a beautiful material that is impossible to patch locally becomes a real headache for whoever maintains the site.

commonMistakes: Choosing a material based purely on how it looks in a photo
Ignoring accessibility and safety underfoot
Forgetting long-term maintenance and repair considerations
followUps: Would your answer change for a rural footpath versus a busy city centre street?

question: How would you design a public garden so it genuinely works for people with limited mobility, not just technically meets the regulations?
lookingFor: Understanding that inclusive design goes beyond minimum compliance to genuine usability and dignity.

bullets: Mention concrete features, gentle gradients, seating at intervals, firm level surfaces, clear signage
Distinguish between meeting minimum legal standards and actually creating a comfortable, dignified experience
Show awareness that involving people with lived experience in the design process improves the outcome
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would want gentle gradients rather than the steepest ramp regulations technically allow, with places to rest every so often, because meeting the minimum standard on paper does not always mean the space actually feels comfortable to use. Firm, even surfaces and clear, uncluttered sightlines matter just as much as any ramp does. I think the best way to actually get this right is to involve people with mobility needs directly in reviewing the design, because they will notice things a regulation checklist misses.

commonMistakes: Treating regulatory compliance as the entire goal
Only mentioning wheelchair access and ignoring other mobility or sensory needs
No mention of involving actual users in the design process
followUps: What is the difference between a space that is accessible and one that is genuinely inclusive?

question: Landscape architects work on everything from a single garden to a whole regional masterplan. Which scale interests you most, and why?
lookingFor: Self-awareness about their own interests within the field's wide range, backed by reasoning.

bullets: Pick a scale honestly, without assuming bigger automatically sounds more impressive
Explain what specifically draws them to that scale of work
Show awareness that the skills and problems differ across scales
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I am drawn to the neighbourhood and city scale, things like a network of parks or a regenerated high street, because I like seeing how a design decision affects how a whole community actually moves through their day. I know that is a very different skill set from designing one perfect private garden, it is more about systems and negotiation between different stakeholders than pure detailed craft. That said, I know I would need to build up from smaller, more detailed projects first to really understand how design decisions play out on the ground.

commonMistakes: Assuming the largest scale is automatically the most impressive answer
Giving no genuine reason for the preference
Showing no awareness that different scales require different skills
followUps: What is one skill you think you would need to build before working at that scale?

question: A client wants you to remove a group of mature, healthy trees to make room for a new building extension. How would you approach that?
lookingFor: Structured ethical and professional reasoning that weighs the client's needs against environmental and long-term value.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine tension between the client's needs and the ecological, amenity value of mature trees
Propose exploring alternatives before accepting removal as inevitable, redesigning footprint, retention, replanting ratios
Show willingness to advise honestly even if it is not what the client wants to hear
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct would not be to just accept the brief as fixed, mature trees take decades to grow and provide value a sapling cannot replace for a very long time, so I would want to properly explore whether the building footprint could shift or be reduced to save them. If removal genuinely could not be avoided, I would want to be honest with the client about that cost, not just environmentally but often in terms of how residents or planners might react, and push for a serious replacement planting strategy rather than a token gesture. I think part of the professional responsibility here is not simply doing what the client first asks, but helping them see the trade-off clearly before they commit to it.

commonMistakes: Immediately agreeing to remove the trees without exploring alternatives
Refusing to consider the client's needs or budget at all
Treating tree removal as purely a technical matter with no ethical dimension
followUps: What would you do if, after all that, the client still insisted on removing the trees?

question: What have you read, watched or visited outside of school that has shaped your interest in landscape architecture?
lookingFor: Genuine evidence of independent exploration of the subject, however small, with real reflection.

bullets: Name something specific, a book, documentary, exhibition or place actually engaged with
Explain what idea or detail from it actually stuck with them
Connect it to how it shaped their thinking or plans going forward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Ian McHarg's Design with Nature over the summer, and while some of it felt dated, the core idea of layering maps, geology, hydrology, ecology, to let the land itself suggest where development should and should not go really stuck with me. It made me start looking at ordinary places differently, wondering why a road or a housing estate ended up exactly where it did. I have also been visiting local parks with a notebook since then, trying to work out what decisions the original designer must have made.

commonMistakes: Naming a source but being unable to say anything specific about its content
Only mentioning something assigned by a teacher with no independent exploration
Giving no connection between the source and their own thinking
followUps: Was there anything in what you read that you disagreed with?

question: Why did you choose to apply for landscape architecture here specifically, rather than another course or university?
lookingFor: Specific, researched motivation tied to the actual course, not generic praise that could fit anywhere.

bullets: Name a specific feature of the course, studio structure, staff research, fieldwork, accreditation
Connect that feature to a concrete personal interest or experience
Show they understand what makes this course different from other options they considered
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at your second year studio brief on post-industrial site regeneration, and that is almost exactly the kind of project that first got me interested, reworking a place with a difficult history rather than starting on a blank field. I also noticed the course runs regular fieldwork trips rather than keeping everything studio-based, which matters to me because I learn best by actually standing on a site. I looked at a couple of other courses too, but this one had the clearest link between the technical modules and real project work, which is exactly the balance I am looking for.

commonMistakes: Giving praise generic enough to apply to any university's course
Leaning only on rankings or reputation with no specific detail
Being unable to name anything distinctive about the actual course structure
followUps: What would you want to contribute to the course as a student?
